subject: Application - Senior Platform Engineer, Observability (Amsterdam)
paragraphs: I am applying for the Senior Platform Engineer - Observability role. The premise of the description is the one I have been building toward for four years: an observability platform whose users are hundreds of product teams, where the engineering job is to stop alerts from firing rather than to answer them faster. My fleet is three orders of magnitude smaller than fifteen hundred servers, but the loop is the same loop, and I have run it end to end rather than read about it.

One flake declares thirteen NixOS hosts, with an SSH certificate authority, SOPS-encrypted secrets and a task interface as the only operator surface. A sentinel records job status, generation age, disk and pressure-stall figures to a ledger every fifteen minutes and pages when a state is not ok — pressure stall being the kernel signal that a machine is thrashing before anything visibly breaks. A change counts only once a gate has read the built artifact back, which is how changes to hosts and services stay safe and predictable instead of hopeful. When something does break I am in journald, nftables and TLS handshakes, and the services on the platform are Go and Python, with a PostgreSQL-backed mail archive among them.

The gaps are worth stating before an interview finds them. I have not run Kubernetes in production: my hosts are single-tenant and separated by role, so kubectl, StatefulSets, Ingress and quota guardrails would be reading rather than operating for me today. I have not operated Elasticsearch, Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics or Tempo — the metrics store I know best is one I designed myself, and tuning a telemetry store at petabyte scale is a different craft from keeping thirteen hosts honest. My fleet is thirteen machines on hardware I own, not fifteen hundred across bare metal and cloud regions. And on the ten years: mine are ten years of engineering across energy and software, not a decade inside observability specifically.

Amsterdam office-first is a decision I would make deliberately, so I should be as direct about the move as about the stack. I am in south-west Germany, and this would be a relocation: I hold German permanent residence and it does not transfer, so the Netherlands route would be a permit sponsored through Adyen as a recognised sponsor, which I would want to plan openly with your mobility team rather than discover at offer stage. I am ready to be in the office and to move for it. What draws me to this team rather than another platform role is that observability is where cost, cardinality and truth about a system all meet, and the guardrail work — stopping one noisy tenant from destabilising everyone else — is the part I would want to own first.
